Chapter 1: How Pornography Shapes the Way People See Women
Picture this—a group of friends, maybe flipping through magazines or catching a late-night show, laughing it off without a second thought. For lots of us, those images just blend into the background of everyday life. But what if there’s more going on beneath the surface?
The way women are shown in these pictures—posed, exposed, and arranged for someone else’s pleasure—starts to influence how people see women, period. It goes way beyond what’s on the page or the screen. Those images start teaching everyone what women are supposed to be, and even what they’re supposedly for.
Most of the time, we don’t even stop to ask why these images pop up everywhere. Maybe a teenager sees a billboard on the way to school. Someone scrolls past an online ad. Or a woman catches herself comparing her own body to what’s being shown.
All of these little moments add up. The message might be subtle, but it’s relentless: women’s bodies are there to be looked at, judged, and used. And honestly, this isn’t just about desire or sex—it’s about power.
Pornography isn’t just off in its own corner—it’s woven right into society. It shapes how we talk, what we expect, and how we treat each other. In these images, women are often reduced to objects—something to be taken, controlled, or consumed.
And the people behind these images? They know what they’re doing. They’re not just selling a product—they’re selling an idea. An idea about what it means to be a woman, and what it means to be a man.
For a lot of people, the line between fantasy and reality gets fuzzy. A young man might grow up thinking this is what sex is supposed to look like. And a woman might feel pressure to look or act a certain way, even if it doesn’t feel right. These images become a kind of script, teaching everyone their lines before they even realize it.
Most of us don’t notice how deep this really goes. It’s not just about what’s on a screen. It’s about what happens when those ideas spill over into the real world. The way women are treated at work, in relationships, even walking down the street—it all gets shaped, bit by bit, by these images.
When women are shown as things to be used, it honestly becomes easier for others to treat them that way.
There’s a quiet pain that comes with this. Some women learn to hide parts of themselves, to shrink away from attention, or just accept things that make them feel small. Others push back, but the weight of these images is tough to shake. The world keeps repeating the same story, until it almost feels like there’s no other story to tell.
But you know what? It doesn’t have to stay this way. Once people start noticing the patterns—once they see how these images shape everything around us—something starts to shift. The first step is spotting the problem, not just in magazines or movies, but in the way we think and act every single day.
And only then, can things really start to change.
